newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka local polls campaign to end at midnight.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka local polls campaign to end at midnight.

text.p: Sri Lankan political parties campaigned feverishly on Tuesday ahead of the midnight deadline to end canvassing for the March 21 local council elections.

"No campaigning will be allowed from midnight on Tuesday and police have been instructed to tear down posters, party symbols and cut-outs which adorn practically every street corner," Deputy Elections Commissioner A.D. de Silva told Reuters.
He said slogan-carrying convoys of candidates, often with pop music blaring over loudspeakers, also must stop, much to the relief of many residents.

"These people have been invading our homes and our privacy and making a complete nuisance of themselves for the past month," said Suresh de Silva, a resident of Nugegoda in the suburbs of Colombo. "I am glad this campaigning bit is over."
But the Indian Ocean island's main political parties made the most of the last few hours, lobbying for the vote in a final series of rallies and street parades.

The ruling People's Alliance (PA) coalition led by President Chandrika Kumaratunga, which is fielding candidates for all of the 228 councils up for grabs, organised its final rally on the outskirts of Colombo.

Kumaratunga, who is under threat of assassination by separatist minority Tamil guerrillas, has made many unannounced appearances at PA rallies since February 5 when nominations for the election closed.
The Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam are fighting for an independent homeland for minority Tamils in this predominantly Sinhalese island.
Occasional no-shows by the president have often left the crowds disappointed, prompting Kumaratunga to address some rallies by telephone.
The poll is the first popularity test for the PA, which in 1994 ended the main opposition United National Party's (UNP) 17 years rule, winning both the general and presidential polls.
The UNP, which controlled about 75 percent of the councils before they were dissolved in January, said it was confident of retaining most of them.
"We feel people will rally round us again," said P. Dayaratne, senior UNP legislator and chairman of the party's campaign coordinating committee.
"We lost in 1994 not because our policies were bad. It was because 17 years was just too long and people wanted a change. Even your parents get tired of you after 17 years," he said.
The election campaign has been marred by violence, beginning with the killing last month of a PA lawmaker during a roadside quarrel between his supporters and UNP activists.
A UNP member of parliament and a former UNP mayor are among the suspects detained by police in connection with the killing.

The Centre for Monitoring Election Violence, an independent monitoring group, said about 1,000 incidents of poll-related violence have been reported since last month. The highest number of allegations were made against the PA, it said.

Nearly 20,000 candidates from 12 political parties and 132 independent groups are contesting Friday's poll throughout the country except in the northern and eastern provinces, where government forces are battling the rebels.
Seats for councils in 12 cities, 31 town and 195 villages are up for election. The size of the councils range from nine seats in remote villages to 53 in Colombo.
